heading: Verify a seller’s rental revenue before relying on the listing
body:
A short-term rental listing may show gross bookings, platform payouts, projected revenue, or a seller’s own spreadsheet. Those figures answer different questions. Before using the advertised revenue in an offer model, request a period-by-period reconciliation showing what guests booked, what was refunded, what fees were withheld, and what cash reached the owner.

Compare the same property and the same period

Check the address, listing identity, dates, and number of nights available. Identify owner stays, maintenance closures, discounted bookings, taxes, cleaning charges, and cancellations. A calendar with many blocked nights does not establish that those nights were paid reservations. An annual estimate does not establish actual operating history.

For a fictional listing advertising $120,000 of revenue, ask whether that amount includes $18,000 of cleaning charges and $8,000 later refunded. If both are included, $94,000 remains before considering platform fees and operating expenses. The example is a reconciliation, not a profitability forecast. Use source records to determine the actual categories.

Separate past performance from what transfers

Ask which furniture, vendor relationships, future reservations, listing assets, and operating records are included in the transaction, and verify transfer rules directly with the relevant platform and professionals. Do not assume that purchasing the real estate transfers an account, reviews, permits, or future bookings.

Build the purchase model from verified revenue and independently priced expenses. Mark anything that remains a seller claim. A property can still be worth investigating when information is incomplete, but the offer and diligence plan should reflect that uncertainty. Use the site’s buyer research to organize the questions before committing funds.

Build an offer file that shows what is still unverified

A useful buyer file separates documents received from conclusions supported. A seller can supply a record without that record answering the purchase question. Keep the property identity, relevant period, reviewer, and unresolved issue beside each document so that a promising listing does not become an assumed fact.

  1. Reconcile the revenue definition. Use the seller revenue-definition crosswalk to compare figures on the same basis. Mark cleaning charges, taxes, refunds, fees, and the period covered before comparing a booking total with a payout or an annual projection.
  2. Track requests to the decision deadline. The seller document-request status board distinguishes requested, received, and reviewed evidence. Identify which missing answer could change price, scope, or whether you proceed. Review contract deadlines with your transaction professionals.
  3. Connect inspection findings to follow-up evidence. Record the question, the relevant report or photograph, and the requested specialist assessment or quote. Use the inspection follow-up evidence board so that an item described as addressed still has supporting documentation.
  4. Identify what the sale includes. A photograph is not an inventory agreement. Use the conveying-item identifier register to describe the specific items being discussed and the records that support their inclusion. Confirm the executed terms with the people handling the transaction.

Before handing the property to a designer or launch team, carry unresolved purchase questions into the buyer-to-design handoff. State what remains unknown, who owns the next action, and which work depends on the answer. These tools support due diligence; they do not verify a listing or replace property-specific professional review.
